title: Few-Step Boltzmann Generators via Scalable Likelihood Flow Maps

paper.title: Few-Step Boltzmann Generators via Scalable Likelihood Flow Maps
paper.abstract:
Abstract Recent progress in flow-based generative modeling has led to models that output high-quality samples while using only a small number of function evaluations. However, at present, there is a lack of similar advances in estimating the
model likelihood.
In particular, most existing methods
either rely on restrictive architectures that enable exact calculations, or use stochastic approximations such as Hutchinson’s trace estimator that introduce substantial variance.
In this work, we introduce SCAlable LikeLihood distillation of flOw maPs ( SCALLOP ). SCALLOP builds on the recently proposed F2D2, a likelihood flow map model that can generate samples and their densities in a small number of function evaluations. While F2D2 uses Hutchinson’s estimator during training, we introduce an alternative and more scalable likelihood distillation objective that is Hutchinson-free and admits a vectorized formulation.
Empirically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SCALLOP as a Boltzmann generator in molecular science, and further validate its benefit on image datasets. SCALLOP significantly reduces both training variance and training time while consistently improving performance compared to F2D2, and is competitive with the state-of-the-art while achieving up to 10 × 10\times inference speedup over the fastest baseline.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: While the generative modeling community’s focus has indexed on improving the empirical quality of generated samples and the speed of generation ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Lu and Song, 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Boffi et al., 2026 ) , numerous applications, notably in the sciences, require access to the model likelihood, e.g., for free energy estimation and enhanced sampling methods ( Torrie and Valleau, 1977 ; Grubmüller, 1995 ; Laio and Parrinello, 2002 ; Barducci et al., 2008 ; Noé et al., 2019 ; Rissanen et al., 2025 ; Nam et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) . To satisfy this requirement, early approaches restricted model architectures to ensure strict invertibility ( Papamakarios et al., 2021 ) , which inherently limits expressivity. Conversely, continuous flow- and diffusion-based models—along with their few-step distilled counterparts—offer far greater expressivity but do not trivially admit scalable likelihood evaluation. Computing their likelihoods remains bottlenecked by either prohibitively expensive Jacobian calculations ( Chen et al., 2019 ; Rehman et al., 2026 ) or high-variance stochastic estimators ( Grathwohl et al., 2018 ) .

sections.heading: Current Approaches and Limitations
sections.text: Overall, the generative modelling literature has focused on learning a transport map from Gaussian samples to data samples, and then using the change-of-variables formula to compute the corresponding likelihood. Using that formula is often problematic: it requires computing costly quantities based on the neural network, during inference or training. Likelihoods of normalizing flows ( Rezende and Mohamed, 2015 ; Papamakarios et al., 2021 ) have limited expressivity and can be slow to compute. Normalizing flows parameterize transport maps as compositions of invertible neural network layers and compute likelihoods through the static change-of-variables formula, which requires evaluating their Jacobian log-determinants. To make this computation cheap, namely linear in the data dimension, the neural network has strong architectural constraints. These constraints can substantially reduce expressivity ( Gao et al., 2020 ) , particularly in applications with important symmetries such as molecular and materials modeling, where autoregressive layers are often unsuitable. For practical applications, expressive architectures require many neural network layers. For example, normalizing flows based on scalable transformer-based architectures ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) have been successfully applied to atomic systems ( Tan et al., 2026a ; Tan et al., 2026b ; Schebek et al., 2025 ) . Still, at inference time, they often suffer from a trade-off in speed between generating samples and computing likelihoods. Computing likelihoods from continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) ( Chen et al., 2019 ) typically suffers from high variance. CNFs remove the architectural constraints of normalizing flows by parameterizing the velocity field of a continuous transport process. Likelihood computation then requires integrating the divergence of the velocity field along trajectories through the instantaneous change-of-variables formula ( Chen et al., 2019 ) . In practice, this divergence is typically estimated using the Hutchinson’s trace estimator ( Grathwohl et al., 2018 ) , whose variance can become prohibitively large in high dimensions: maintaining constant precision may require computational budgets scaling quadratically with the data dimension. While variance-reduction techniques have been developed ( Meyer et al., ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , they are not mainstream. Recent CNF distillation methods struggle to reconcile fast sampling with scalable and tractable likelihood evaluation. For instance, while flow map models ( Boffi et al., 2025 ) successfully compress sampling into a single forward pass, they do not natively support tractable likelihood evaluation. Unlike standard normalizing flows, these models lack explicit architectural constraints and are not guaranteed to be bijective. To address this, subsequent works attempt to enforce model invertibility via regularization techniques ( Draxler et al., 2024 ; Rehman et al., 2026 ) ; however, likelihood evaluation under these models remains computationally expensive—scaling cubically with the data dimension ( 𝒪 ⁡ ( d 3 ) \mathcal{O}(d^{3}) ) due to the required Jacobian log-determinant calculation. To bypass this bottleneck, Ai et al. (2026) frame likelihood evaluation as a parallel distillation task, jointly amortizing both the sampling process and the likelihood estimation into a few network evaluations. Nevertheless, training this joint architecture still relies on Hutchinson-based divergence estimators, thereby inheriting their characteristic high variance. Alternatively, energy-based parameterizations of CNFs ( Aggarwal et al., 2025 ; OuYang et al., 2026a ; Plainer et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ; Guth et al., 2026 ) enable likelihood estimation in a single network evaluation, while they are not capable to generate samples in few steps.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: In this work, we build on F2D2 ( Ai et al., 2026 ) that extends flow maps into likelihood flow maps that distill both the sampling procedure and the likelihood computation into a single neural network evaluation. We propose SCAlable LikeLihood distillation of flOw maPs ( SCALLOP ), which replaces the likelihood distillation loss in F2D2 with an alternative, based on reformulating the change-of-density along the flow. Our contributions are as follows: • Our new training objective makes likelihood distillation more scalable by design. It has lower-variance because it is Hutchinson-free and faster to optimize given the “vectorized" formulation of our objective. • Empirical improvements over the F2D2 model, on which SCALLOP is based, are substantial: SCALLOP can reduce training variance by up to 100 × 100\times , converges faster, and consistently obtains better test set performance. • In molecular domains, SCALLOP is much faster than state-of-the-art Boltzmann Generators at inference time: 10 × 10\times faster than normalizing flows ( Tan et al., 2026a ) while achieving better performance, and 100 × 100\times faster than the comparable FALCON ( Rehman et al., 2026 ) . • These empirical gains translate to higher-dimensional image domains, where SCALLOP estimates more accurate likelihoods than F2D2, while being faster and more stable to train.

sections.text: We motivate our study with a common setting: A practitioner is interested in sampling from an unnormalized distribution π \pi to approximate some macroscopic property like free energy differences, denoted O O . π \pi takes on a Boltzmann distribution and the observable O O is computed in expectation: π ⁡ ( x ) = 1 Z ​ exp ⁡ ( − U ⁡ ( x ) ) , 𝔼 π ​ [ O ⁡ ( X ) ] = ∫ O ⁡ ( x ) ​ π ​ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x , \displaystyle\pi(x)=\frac{1}{Z}\exp({-U(x)}),\quad\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[O(X)]=\int O(x)\pi(x)\,dx, (1) where U : ℝ d → ℝ U:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is the energy and Z Z is a normalizing constant. Since drawing unbiased samples from the Boltzmann distribution is difficult, Boltzmann Generators ( Noé et al., 2019 ) fit a generative model p θ p^{\theta} to a potentially biased, accessible distribution p data p_{\text{data}} with similarities to π \pi . Then p θ p^{\theta} approximates O O with self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS): 𝔼 π ​ [ O ​ ( X ) ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[O(X)] = 𝔼 p θ ​ [ π ⁡ ( X ) p θ ​ ( X ) ​ O ​ ( X ) ] ≈ ∑ n = 1 N w n ​ x n ∑ m = 1 N w m , where ​ w n = exp ⁡ ( − U ⁡ ( x n ) ) p θ ​ ( x n ) , x n ∼ p θ . \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p^{\theta}}\left[\frac{\pi(X)}{p^{\theta}(X)}O(X)\right]\approx\frac{\sum_{n=1}^{N}w_{n}x_{n}}{\sum_{m=1}^{N}w_{m}},\quad\text{where}w_{n}=\frac{\exp(-U(x_n))}{p^{\theta}(x_{n})},\,x_{n}\sim p^{\theta}. (2) SNIS requires evaluating the probability density of the generated sample x x under p θ p^{\theta} , commonly referred to as the model likelihood. Provided no ambiguity arises, we use the terms sample density and model likelihood interchangeably throughout this paper. Presently, the most expressive generative architectures, such as continuous-time flow models ( Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) , require computationally expensive simulations to evaluate exact densities. Prior works either restrict themselves to less expressive models with tractable likelihoods, or rely on the Hutchinson trace estimator during training or inference. In this work, we present an alternative to the latter: a novel distillation objective for likelihood flow maps that enables simultaneous sample generation and density approximation from continuous-time models without requiring Hutchinson’s trace estimator at any stage . Beyond our primary motivation, efficient likelihood estimation is of broad interest across machine learning, with applications extending to reward tilting and model composition.

sections.heading: 3.5 SCALLOP
sections.text: Combing the training objectives from Section 3.2 with our Conditional Divergence Matching objective ( Section 3.3 ) and the vectorization technique ( Section 3.4 ), we propose SCALLOP , a scalable and efficient pipeline for training a likelihood flow map. The complete training objective is written in Equation 24 . Again, we consider a distillation setting following Ai et al. (2026) , where a pretrained velocity field v t ϕ ≈ v t v_{t}^{\phi}\approx v_{t} is available. When no ambiguity arises, we denote v t v_{t} as v t ϕ v_{t}^{\phi} for notational simplicity. We focus on modelling molecular systems, where specific symmetries must be respected. Related works are discussed in Section 1 and expanded on in Section 7 .

sections.heading: Instantiation.
sections.text: We optimize Equation 24 to train SCALLOP . In particular, we use the LSD loss ( Equation 11 ) as the self distillation loss, and leave the other alternatives for future work.

sections.heading: Molecular Systems.
sections.text: We conduct experiments on several alanine systems of varying lengths, including Alanine Dipeptide (ALA-2), Alanine Tripeptide (ALA-3), Alanine Tetrapeptide (ALA-4), and Alanine Hexapeptide (ALA-6). Data are obtained from simulating Molecular Dynamics in implicit solvent, with the AMBER-14 force field. Details of the simulation are provided in Section 8 . Following Tan et al. (2026a) ; Rehman et al. (2026) , models are trained on the biased dataset. The goal is to correct the model using self-normalized importance sampling, enabling it to sample equilibrium conformations corresponding to the Boltzmann distribution.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We benchmark SCALLOP against the most promising discrete- and continuous- flow baselines identified by Rehman et al. (2026) : SBG ( Tan et al., 2026a ) and FALCON ( Rehman et al., 2026 ) . Specifically, to better focus on likelihood evaluation, we compare against the SBG with standard SNIS (denoted as SBG-IS). Although an SMC-based variant (SBG-SMC) exists and can be seamlessly integrated with both FALCON and SCALLOP , we exclude it from our current benchmark to ensure fair comparison with SNIS, leaving the exploration of SCALLOP -SMC for future work.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: We evaluate SCALLOP and the baselines using standard SNIS. To measure sampling efficiency, we report the Effective Sample Size (ESS). To quantify the effectiveness of the reweighted samples, we compute the 2-Wasserstein distance for both the distributions of energy ( ℰ ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathcal{E}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} ) and torsional angle ( 𝕋 ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathbb{T}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} ). Specifically, ℰ ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathcal{E}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} is sensitive to extreme energy values—often caused by atoms being too close to one another—and thus reflects local structural refinements. Conversely, because torsional angles act as the primary collective variables capturing the most information in alanine systems, 𝕋 ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathbb{T}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} measures global structural quality. Further details are provided in Appendix 8 .

sections.heading: Comparable Performance against SOTA.
sections.text: The performance of SCALLOP and the other baselines are reported in Table 1 . Across different systems, SCALLOP consistently outperforms F2D2 across all considered metrics, while achieving highly competitive results against the state-of-the-art FALCON and FALCON-A. Specifically, SCALLOP excels at capturing the global conformational space, achieving the best 𝕋 ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathbb{T}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} on the ALA-3 and ALA-6 systems. Furthermore, it consistently yields a high ESS, indicating substantial overlap with the target distribution and a strong resistance to mode collapse—a conclusion further corroborated by its strong 𝕋 ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathbb{T}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} performance. While FALCON generally achieves a lower ℰ ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathcal{E}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} , SCALLOP drastically improves upon F2D2, nearly halving the ℰ ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathcal{E}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} error in larger systems like ALA-4 and ALA-6. More importantly, higher ℰ ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathcal{E}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} values do not undermine the overall validity of the drawn samples, as the Wasserstein-2 distance is notoriously sensitive to energy outliers caused by microscopic structural deviations. The low 𝕋 ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathbb{T}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} demonstrates that SCALLOP correctly captures the global torsional angle structure, confirming that the macroscopic metastable states and their statistical weights are accurately recovered. Because the underlying conformational macrostates are correct, the remaining local structural noise that inflates the ℰ ​ - ​ 𝒲 2 \mathcal{E}\text{-}\mathcal{W}_{2} can be efficiently mitigated by applying a computationally cheap local relaxation to align the local structures. sections.heading: 4.2 Effectiveness and Scalability beyond Molecules
sections.text: To test whether the benefits of SCALLOP generalize beyond molecular data, we evaluate it on unconditional image generation using CelebA-64 ( Liu et al., 2015 ) . Following the F2D2 evaluation protocol, we report FID for sample quality and BPD, i.e., negative log-likelihood measured in bits per dimension, for likelihood estimation. We further report the absolute deviation from the 1024-step teacher BPD and the mean absolute per-sample BPD error with respect to the same teacher reference. All metrics are evaluated using 1, 2, 4, and 8 Euler steps for both sampling and likelihood computation. As shown in Table 2 , SCALLOP achieves BPD and FID comparable to F2D2 across all steps, while consistently reducing the per-sample BPD error. Figure 7 further shows that SCALLOP has more stable training dynamics, with lower variance in both training loss and gradient norm compared with F2D2 over 60k training steps. Moreover, its loss computation takes only 83.1 % 83.1\% of the wall-clock time of F2D2, demonstrating improved computational efficiency. Additional details are provided in Section 10 .

sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: In conclusion, we proposed SCAlable LikeLihood distillation of flOw maPs ( SCALLOP ), an efficient procedure for training few-step models to jointly generate samples and their densities. This capability allows SCALLOP to serve as a Boltzmann generator for sampling from unnormalized densities, where it is competitive with the state-of-the-art while being significantly faster to evaluate at inference time.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Despite its empirical success, SCALLOP has two main limitations. First, the conditional divergence matching objective relies on the assumption that the velocity is perfectly learnt, while the theoretical gap and resulting bias currently remain unquantified. Second, while SCALLOP can generate samples and their densities in 1 1 step, it practically uses ∼ 10 \sim 10 steps for high-dimensional tasks.

sections.heading: Notation and Terminology.
sections.text: Throughout this appendix, we operate within the framework of generative modeling via continuous-time paths. Here, x 0 x_{0} and x 1 x_{1} denote the endpoint data variables, x t x_{t} represents the intermediate state at time t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] , and z z is the latent noise variable driving the process. Unless otherwise specified, conditional expectations of the form 𝔼 [ ⋅ | x t ] \mathbb{E}[\cdot|x_{t}] are taken over the joint posterior distribution p ⁡ ( x 0 , x 1 | x t ) p(x_{0},x_{1}|x_{t}) of the endpoints given the intermediate state. Because the noise z z is uniquely determined once ( x 0 , x 1 , x t ) (x_{0},x_{1},x_{t}) are known, expectations involving the noise (such as 𝔼 ⁡ [ z | x t ] \mathbb{E}[z|x_{t}] ) are implicitly evaluated under this same posterior. Furthermore, we adopt a slight abuse of terminology for convenience: we frequently refer to analytical formulas containing exact population expectations as “estimators.” Strictly speaking, these mathematical expressions represent theoretical population limits. In practice, it is understood that these exact expectations are substituted with their corresponding unbiased finite-sample estimators via empirical Monte Carlo averages over mini-batches during training.

sections.heading: 7 Expanded Discussion of Related Works
sections.text: The following are three dominant approaches used in computational chemistry for training neural networks that support efficient sampling and likelihood. Once such neural networks are trained, they can be used as a proposal distribution, known in computational chemistry as a Boltzmann generator, for self-normalized importance sampling of a Boltzmann distribution.

sections.heading: Discrete and Continuous Normalizing Flows
sections.text: Boltzmann Generators (BGs) are tractable proposal distributions used in importance sampling, allowing both efficient sampling and likelihood evaluation. They were first applied to molecular systems by Noé et al. (2019) , who parameterized them using neural networks in the form of Normalizing Flows (NFs). Subsequent work has evolved along two main directions. The first replaces NFs with their continuous counterpart, Continuous Normalizing Flows ( Chen et al., 2019 , CNFs) that can be parameterized using more flexible model architectures. For instance, Köhler et al. (2020) ; Klein et al. (2023) develop equivariant CNFs tailored to molecular systems. However, this approach does not scale well: computing the log-likelihood requires integrating the divergence of the velocity field (as in Eq. 3 ), which becomes prohibitively expensive in high dimensions. The second direction instead focuses on improving the expressivity and sampling efficiency of standard NFs. Recent work, such as TarFlow ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) , introduces scalable transformer-based architectures, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Building on this line, Tan et al. (2026a) ; Tan et al. (2026b) ; Schebek et al. (2025) pushed the boundaries of NFs for atomic systems. In particular, Tan et al. (2026a) also proposes an inference-time scaling strategy to further improve sampling efficiency.

sections.heading: Energy-based Diffusion Models.
sections.text: Training diffusion models with energy parameterization acts a bridge to alleviate the computational overhead of solving the divergence integration in CNFs, where the learned energies define Boltzmann distributions on different noise levels. Recent works focus on improving energy-based diffusion models training beyond Denoising Score Matching. Aggarwal et al. (2025) ; OuYang et al. (2026a) incorporate Noise-Contrastive Estimation ( Gutmann and Hyvärinen, 2012 ) , where Aggarwal et al. (2025) treats the learned energy of clean data as the approximated normalized likelihood and OuYang et al. (2026a) leverages the learned intermediate energies for further inference-time control. He et al. (2026) improves the training via imposing the Bayes’ rule constraint, with an application of the EBMs for free energy estimation. Plainer et al. (2026) regularizes the EBMs to enforce the Fokker-Planck Equation, and uses the learned EBMs as a force field. Yu et al. (2026) proposes a unified framework for learning EBMs. In contrast to the standard data-driven setting, OuYang et al. (2026b) proposes an energy matching objective for learning a Boltzmann neural sampler when data is unavailable, relying instead on the unnormalized target density.

sections.heading: Flow Maps with Approximate Invertibility.
sections.text: NFs enables exact likelihood evaluation through its invertibility, which also limits its flexibility. To enable the usage of more flexible network architecture, Free-form Flows ( Draxler et al., 2024 ) propose to softly enforce the invertibility through an additional reconstruction loss. To incorporate with the recent advanced few-steps generative models, FALCON ( Rehman et al., 2026 ) proposes to make flow map invertible, by additionally imposing reconstruction losses on the jump between two times t < s t<s . FALCON enables flow map to have fast yet accurate likelihood estimation and shows its effectiveness and scalability on molecular systems. However, FALCON requires the exact log-determinant of the Jacobian of the flow map for likelihood evaluation; over T T steps, this is computationally expensive, resulting in 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(Td) function evaluations and an additional 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ​ d 3 ) \mathcal{O}(Td^{3}) cost.

sections.heading: Hyperparameter for Training.
sections.text: We train all models with an exponential moving average (EMA) on the weights using a decay rate of 0.999. We use the AdamW optimizer with learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , gradient-norm clip 10 10 , and weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} . We employ a square-root annealing learning rate schedule with a warm-up phase covering 2.5 2.5 % of the training iterations. All trainings are using batch size 1000 1000 , with 4 × 10 6 4\times 10^{6} updates in total.

sections.heading: Data Augmentation.
sections.text: To preserve SE(3) symmetries, we employ the Center-of-Mass adjustment and standardlize the data using mean and std estimated from the training set. We further employ random rotation to the data every time it is sampled, to enforce soft constraint on the rotational equivariance.

sections.heading: Hyperparameters.
sections.text: In all evaluations, we draw 2 × 10 5 2\times 10^{5} samples from the model and employ SNIS for resampling. In SNIS, logit values are clipped at 0.002, as in standard baselines ( Tan et al., 2026a ; Tan et al., 2026b ; Rehman et al., 2026 ) . We use batch size 10 4 10^{4} for both SCALLOP , F2D2, and SBG-IS during inference to maximize GPU utility, for all benchmarks. However, FALCON only fits with significant smaller batch size due to the need of exact Jacobian calculation. On a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, FALCON only fits batch size (1000, 1000, 500, 100) for ALA-(2, 3, 4, 6), respectively. We employ an linear schedule for all generation in SCALLOP and F2D2.

Boffi Pradeep Ravikumar José Miguel Hernández-Lobato Max Simchowitz Benjamin Kurt Miller Omar Chehab Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Abstract Recent progress in flow-based generative modeling has led to models that output high-quality samples while using only a small number of function evaluations. However, at present, there is a lack of similar advances in estimating the model likelihood. In particular, most existing methods either rely on restrictive architectures that enable exact calculations, or use stochastic approximations such as Hutchinson’s trace estimator that introduce substantial variance. In this work, we introduce SCAlable LikeLihood distillation of flOw maPs ( SCALLOP ). SCALLOP builds on the recently proposed F2D2, a likelihood flow map model that can generate samples and their densities in a small number of function evaluations. While F2D2 uses Hutchinson’s estimator during training, we introduce an alternative and more scalable likelihood distillation objective that is Hutchinson-free and admits a vectorized formulation. Empirically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SCALLOP as a Boltzmann generator in molecular science, and further validate its benefit on image datasets. SCALLOP significantly reduces both training variance and training time while consistently improving performance compared to F2D2, and is competitive with the state-of-the-art while achieving up to 10 × 10	imes inference speedup over the fastest baseline. 1 Introduction While the generative modeling community’s focus has indexed on improving the empirical quality of generated samples and the speed of generation ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ; Lu and Song, 2025 ; Geng et al., 2025 ; Boffi et al., 2026 ) , numerous applications, notably in the sciences, require access to the model likelihood, e.g., for free energy estimation and enhanced sampling methods ( Torrie and Valleau, 1977 ; Grubmüller, 1995 ; Laio and Parrinello, 2002 ; Barducci et al., 2008 ; Noé et al., 2019 ; Rissanen et al., 2025 ; Nam et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) . To satisfy this requirement, early approaches restricted model architectures to ensure strict invertibility ( Papamakarios et al., 2021 ) , which inherently limits expressivity. Conversely, continuous flow- and diffusion-based models—along with their few-step distilled counterparts—offer far greater expressivity but do not trivially admit scalable likelihood evaluation. Computing their likelihoods remains bottlenecked by either prohibitively expensive Jacobian calculations ( Chen et al., 2019 ; Rehman et al., 2026 ) or high-variance stochastic estimators ( Grathwohl et al., 2018 ) . Current Approaches and Limitations Overall, the generative modelling literature has focused on learning a transport map from Gaussian samples to data samples, and then using the change-of-variables formula to compute the corresponding likelihood. Using that formula is often problematic: it requires computing costly quantities based on the neural network, during inference or training. Likelihoods of normalizing flows ( Rezende and Mohamed, 2015 ; Papamakarios et al., 2021 ) have limited expressivity and can be slow to compute. Normalizing flows parameterize transport maps as compositions of invertible neural network layers and compute likelihoods through the static change-of-variables formula, which requires evaluating their Jacobian log-determinants. To make this computation cheap, namely linear in the data dimension, the neural network has strong architectural constraints. These constraints can substantially reduce expressivity ( Gao et al., 2020 ) , particularly in applications with important symmetries such as molecular and materials modeling, where autoregressive layers are often unsuitable. For practical applications, expressive architectures require many neural network layers. For example, normalizing flows based on scalable transformer-based architectures ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) have been successfully applied to atomic systems ( Tan et al., 2026a ; Tan et al., 2026b ; Schebek et al., 2025 ) . Still, at inference time, they often suffer from a trade-off in speed between generating samples and computing likelihoods. Computing likelihoods from continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) ( Chen et al., 2019 ) typically suffers from high variance. CNFs remove the architectural constraints of normalizing flows by parameterizing the velocity field of a continuous transport process. Likelihood computation then requires integrating the divergence of the velocity field along trajectories through the instantaneous change-of-variables formula ( Chen et al., 2019 ) . In practice, this divergence is typically estimated using the Hutchinson’s trace estimator ( Grathwohl et al., 2018 ) , whose variance can become prohibitively large in high dimensions: maintaining constant precision may require computational budgets scaling quadratically with the data dimension. While variance-reduction techniques have been developed ( Meyer et al., ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , they are not mainstream. Recent CNF distillation methods struggle to reconcile fast sampling with scalable and tractable likelihood evaluation. For instance, while flow map models ( Boffi et al., 2025 ) successfully compress sampling into a single forward pass, they do not natively support tractable likelihood evaluation. Unlike standard normalizing flows, these models lack explicit architectural constraints and are not guaranteed to be bijective. To address this, subsequent works attempt to enforce model invertibility via regularization techniques ( Draxler et al., 2024 ; Rehman et al., 2026 ) ; however, likelihood evaluation under these models remains computationally expensive—scaling cubically with the data dimension ( 𝒪 ⁡ ( d 3 ) \mathcal{O}(d^{3}) ) due to the required Jacobian log-determinant calculation. To bypass this bottleneck, Ai et al. (2026) frame likelihood evaluation as a parallel distillation task, jointly amortizing both the sampling process and the likelihood estimation into a few network evaluations. Nevertheless, training this joint architecture still relies on Hutchinson-based divergence estimators, thereby inheriting their characteristic high variance. Alternatively, energy-based parameterizations of CNFs ( Aggarwal et al., 2025 ; OuYang et al., 2026a ; Plainer et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ; Guth et al., 2026 ) enable likelihood estimation in a single network evaluation, while they are not capable to generate samples in few steps. Contributions. In this work, we build on F2D2 ( Ai et al., 2026 ) that extends flow maps into likelihood flow maps that distill both the sampling procedure and the likelihood computation into a single neural network evaluation. We propose SCAlable LikeLihood distillation of flOw maPs ( SCALLOP ), which replaces the likelihood distillation loss in F2D2 with an alternative, based on reformulating the change-of-density along the flow. Our contributions are as follows: • Our new training objective makes likelihood distillation more scalable by design. It has lower-variance because it is Hutchinson-free and faster to optimize given the “vectorized" formulation of our objective. • Empirical improvements over the F2D2 model, on which SCALLOP is based, are substantial: SCALLOP can reduce training variance by up to 100 × 100	imes , converges faster, and consistently obtains better test set performance. • In molecular domains, SCALLOP is much faster than state-of-the-art Boltzmann Generators at inference time: 10 × 10	imes faster than normalizing flows ( Tan et al., 2026a ) while achieving better performance, and 100 × 100	imes faster than the comparable FALCON ( Rehman et al., 2026 ) . • These empirical gains translate to higher-dimensional image domains, where SCALLOP estimates more accurate likelihoods than F2D2, while being faster and more stable to train. 2 Background We motivate our study with a common setting: A practitioner is interested in sampling from an unnormalized distribution π \pi to approximate some macroscopic property like free energy differences, denoted O O . π \pi takes on a Boltzmann distribution and the observable O O is computed in expectation: π ⁡ ( x ) = 1 Z ​ exp ⁡ ( − U ⁡ ( x ) ) , 𝔼 π ​ [ O ⁡ ( X ) ] = ∫ O ⁡ ( x ) ​ π ​ ( x ) ​ 𝑑 x , \displaystyle\pi(x)= rac{1}{Z}\exp({-U(x)}),\quad\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[O(X)]=\int O(x)\pi(x)\,dx, (1) where U : ℝ d → ℝ U:\mathbb{R}^{d}ightarrow\mathbb{R} is the energy and Z Z is a normalizing constant.
